smt-2011-general-01.title: Cycle of three substitutions
smt-2011-general-01.body:
Put $x=2$: $F(2)+F(\frac12)=3$. Put $x=\frac12$: $F(\frac12)+F(-1)=\frac32$. Put $x=-1$: $F(-1)+F(2)=0$. Adding the first and third and subtracting the second: $2F(2)=3+0-\frac32=\frac32$, so $F(2)=\frac34$.

**Answer: $\frac34$**

smt-2011-general-04.title: Cases
smt-2011-general-04.body:
The equation is $|x-1||x^2-2|=2$.

- If $x>\sqrt2$, or $-\sqrt2<x<1$: then $(x-1)(x^2-2)=2$ (for $x>\sqrt2$ both factors are positive; for $-\sqrt2<x<1$ both are negative, so the product is positive and equals $(x-1)(x^2-2)$). This is $x^3-x^2-2x=x(x-2)(x+1)=0$. The roots $x=2$ (valid, $>\sqrt2$), $x=0$ and $x=-1$ (valid, in $(-\sqrt2,1)$).
- If $1<x<\sqrt2$ or $x<-\sqrt2$: then $(1-x)(x^2-2)=2$, i.e. $x^3-x^2-2x+4=0$. By the rational root theorem the only candidates are $\pm1,\pm2,\pm4$, and none of them works.

So the rational roots are $-1,0,2$.

**Answer: $-1,\ 0,\ 2$**

smt-2011-general-06.title: Case analysis
smt-2011-general-06.body:
Suppose $2^a+3^b=c^2$.

*$b=0$:* $2^a=(c-1)(c+1)$, so both factors are powers of $2$ differing by $2$: $c=3$, $a=3$, giving $2^3+3^0=9=3^2$.

*$b\ge1$:* $c^2\equiv2^a\pmod 3$ must be $1$, so $a=2d$ is even. Then $3^b=(c-2^d)(c+2^d)$, so $c-2^d=3^q$ and $c+2^d=3^p$ with $q<p$, $p+q=b$. Subtracting: $2^{d+1}=3^p-3^q$. If $q\ge1$ the right side is divisible by $3$, impossible, so $q=0$ and $3^p-2^{d+1}=1$. By the given fact $p\le2$: $p=1$ gives $d=0$ ($a=0,b=1$: $1+3=4=2^2$) and $p=2$ gives $d=2$ ($a=4,b=2$: $16+9=25=5^2$).

The squares are $4,9,25$.

**Answer: $2^2,3^2,5^2$**

smt-2011-general-07.title: Split at the backward jump
smt-2011-general-07.body:
Let $f_n$ be the number of ways to get from $0$ to $n$ using jumps of $1$ or $2$: $f_0=f_1=1$, $f_n=f_{n-1}+f_{n-2}$, so $f_2,\dots,f_7=2,3,5,8,13,21$.

Suppose the backward jump goes from $n$ to $n-1$. Before it the frog reached $n$ with forward jumps ($f_n$ ways), and afterwards it goes from $n-1$ to $7$ with forward jumps, a distance of $8-n$ ($f_{8-n}$ ways). We need $n\ge1$ (so the frog does not land on $-1$) and $n\le6$ (the frog has not arrived at $7$ before turning). Hence the count is
$$\sum_{n=1}^6f_nf_{8-n}=1\cdot13+2\cdot8+3\cdot5+5\cdot3+8\cdot2+13\cdot1=146.$$

**Answer: 146**

smt-2011-general-08.title: Recursion
smt-2011-general-08.body:
Let $a_n$ be the number of sparse binary strings of length $n$ (leading zeros allowed), i.e. sparse numbers less than $2^n$. Then $a_0=1$, $a_1=2$, $a_2=3$. For $n\ge3$, look at the leading digit: if it is $0$, the rest is any sparse string of length $n-1$; if it is $1$, the next two digits must be $0$ and the rest is any sparse string of length $n-3$. So $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-3}$:
$$a_3=4,\ 6,\ 9,\ 13,\ 19,\ 28,\ 41,\ 60,\ 88,\ 129,\ 189,\ 277,\ 406,\ 595,\ 872$$
for $n=3,\dots,17$. So $a_{17}=872$.

**Answer: 872**

smt-2011-general-14.title: Smallest tangent circle
smt-2011-general-14.body:
For $P=(a,0)$, $\angle MPN$ is the inscribed angle on chord $MN$ in the circle through $M,P,N$, so a larger angle means a smaller circle. The smallest circle through $M$ and $N$ meeting the $x$-axis is tangent to it. Its center lies on the perpendicular bisector $y=3-x$ of $MN$, so it is $(a,3-a)$ with radius $3-a$ (tangent to the $x$-axis at $(a,0)$). Passing through $M$: $(a+1)^2+(1-a)^2=(3-a)^2$, i.e. $a^2+6a-7=0$, $a=1$ or $a=-7$. The radii are $2$ and $10$; the smaller circle gives $a=1$.

**Answer: 1**

smt-2011-general-17.title: Vertex and neighbor
smt-2011-general-17.body:
A rotation of the icosahedron is determined by where it sends a vertex $v$ and one of its $5$ neighbors $w$, and every such pair $(v',w')$ of adjacent vertices is achieved by exactly one rotation. There are $12\cdot5=60$ ordered pairs of adjacent vertices, so there are $60$ rotations.

**Answer: 60**

smt-2011-general-21.title: Sector plus two wrapped quarter-circles
smt-2011-general-21.body:
Put the ant at the corner $O$ of the brick; the brick occupies the quadrant $\{x>0,y<0\}$ near $O$ (brick $[0,1]\times[-1,0]$).

- Leash straight: a $270^\circ$ sector of radius $6$, area $\frac34\cdot36\pi=27\pi$.
- Leash wrapped around the corner $(1,0)$: radius $5$, a quarter disk $\{x\ge1,y\le0\}$ of area $\frac{25\pi}4$. Wrapped around $(0,-1)$: a quarter disk $\{x\ge0,y\le-1\}$, area $\frac{25\pi}4$. (Wrapping around the far corner $(1,-1)$ adds nothing new.)

These two quarter disks overlap in the region $\{x\ge1,y\le-1\}$ within $5$ of both $(1,0)$ and $(0,-1)$. The two circles meet at $D=(4,-4)$. The overlap's area is
$$\int_1^4\left(\sqrt{25-(x-1)^2}-1\right)dx+\int_4^5\sqrt{25-x^2}\,dx=\left(3+\tfrac{25}2x\right)+\left(\tfrac{25}2x-6\right)=25x-3,$$
where $x=\arcsin\frac35=\arctan\frac34$.

Total: $27\pi+\frac{25\pi}2-(25x-3)=\frac{79\pi}2+3-25x\approx111.005$.

**Answer: $\frac{79\pi}2+3-25x$**

smt-2011-general-21.title: Monte Carlo check
smt-2011-general-21.body:
Computing shortest leash paths around the brick for a million random points of the plane and counting those within distance $6$ gives an area of $\approx110.96\pm0.1$, in agreement with $\frac{79\pi}2+3-25\arctan\frac34=111.005\ldots$

**Answer: $\frac{79\pi}2+3-25x$**
